utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Registrar, would you please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say good afternoon to the Office of the Prosecutor. I hope that the interpreters are here. Can everybody hear me now? We can resume at the point where we stopped two weeks ago. The Trial Chamber has rendered two decisions about which we don't have to speak any longer. Having said that, unless there are any preliminary motions, let me turn to Mr. Hayman or to Mr. Nobilo or to Mr. Paley, is it? Paley, yes, that's correct. Excuse me for mispronouncing your name. I'll get used to your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We are prepared to proceed with the Defence case, Mr. President, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can see that you have, indeed, prepared in a significant manner for our discussions this afternoon. I can see that this must have taken a lot of effort and it means you've done a lot of work. I hope it's going to facilitate our work. The floor is yours, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, learned counsel of the Prosecution. In the summer of 1992, when the disintegration of Yugoslavia was underway, Tihomir Blaskic was a captain in the JNA posted to Slovenia. He was the deputy commander of a battalion principally occupied with training and instructing the soldiers in the unit. He had been raised as a small boy in Brestovsko, a village in the Kiseljak municipality. In 1991 and 1992, his parents still resided in the family home in the Kiseljak municipality, but Tihomir Blaskic had left Bosnia at the age of 14 in 1975 to attend higher school and military academy in Zagreb and Belgrade. He spent his formative years, not in rural Bosnia, but in urban, multi-ethnic societies as part of his schooling. At military academy, he shared a room with five other cadets. The six nationalities of the former Yugoslavia were represented in that dormitory room by design. The cadets lived and learned and laughed together. Tihomir Blaskic left the academy with more than a strong appreciation for cultural diversity and the benefits we all obtain from it. As the JNA changed in the 1980s after Tito's death, Tihomir Blaskic's positive views towards multi-ethnicism got him into trouble. In 1985, he was offered a command position in a unit which he believed would be sent to Kosovo. He did not want to go to Kosovo, where the JNA at the time was principally engaged in demonstrations of force against Albanians there, ethnic Albanians. Why, he thought, should a people's army be engaged in shows of force against the people they were sworn to protect? He refused the position he was offered. That refusal resulted in threats by Serb authorities within the JNA of a term in military prison. In August of 1991, a second and more serious crisis ended the JNA career of Captain Blaskic. He saw that the JNA in Slovenia was turning against the Slovene people and he wanted no part of it. He would not participate in a war against the Slovenes and, instead, applied for permission to leave the JNA. The JNA never released him, but he still did not give up his views. He left the JNA in the middle of the night on the 12th of August, 1991 and left the former Yugoslavia entirely. He fled with his wife, Ratka, to Vienna where they lived for the remainder of 1991 and well into 1992. In early 1992, the Croats and Muslims in central Bosnia worked together as allies in preparation for the expected JNA attack. In February of that year, Tihomir Blaskic was contacted by members of the Kiseljak Municipal Council who asked him to return to the area to assist in organising the Defence of Kiseljak. The group that asked him to return was comprised of both Croat and Muslim members. After 17 years away from Bosnia, he was an outsider to that country. His wife, Ratka, had been raised in Austria and her parents lived there. The Blaskics' could easily have remained in Austria with their young son Ivo. In fact, Ratka was opposed to returning to Bosnia. But Tihomir Blaskic decided he could not turn his back on those who needed his help so much, and he agreed to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina for two months only to assist in the preparation of a plan of defence for the Kiseljak municipality. His return to Bosnia-Herzegovina was not an easy journey. While en route to Kiseljak, he was arrested by the JNA and imprisoned. During his imprisonment, he was physically abused by his JNA captors. In mid April, he was released from the Tuzla garrison, the JNA garrison, and he made his way, finally, to his parents home in the Kiseljak municipality. There, he went to see the crisis committee, a mixed ethnic group who asked him to work on a defence plan for the municipality. In the following weeks, he was made the deputy municipal commander of the combined defending forces in Kiseljak, although, in fact, there was no umbrella organisation at the time. There were simply different types of military organisations, such as the Territorial Defence, the Patriotic League, the Municipal Staff and so forth. He shared command of this umbrella organisation, if you will, with another commander, a Muslim named Bakir Alispahic. Although Tihomir Blaskic is charged in the indictment in this case with unspecified war crimes in May and April of 1992, during that time, he shared a joint command with Mr. Alispahic in Kiseljak. Tihomir Blaskic worked for two months preparing defensive plans for Kiseljak. He did not seek out a higher position. Rather, he was recommended by others for the position of the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone of the HVO, and on the 27th of June, 1992, he was appointed to that position. He was given no rank in the HVO, and although the operative zone had existed for only a short period of time, he was the fifth commander to be given that position. Along with the position, he inherited several urgent tasks. His first and foremost responsibility was to defend the operative zone against aggression by the JNA and the Bosnian Serb militia, which had already overrun two-thirds of Bosnia-Herzegovina. His second task was to organise the Bosnian Croat militia or HVO. Although it had been proclaimed on paper, in reality, it did not yet exist. He also had to deal with the existing self-organised and self-armed Croat units and gangs that existed in the territory. All this he had to do with little help from anyone. The national government in Bosnia-Herzegovina was dysfunctional, and at the municipal level, government entities were confused and chaotic. Tihomir Blaskic was a professional soldier told to command a peasant militia. What he found was that there were no trained units in the HVO. The HVO militiamen were loyal to local politicians and were preoccupied with the defence of their own village or even their own homes. There were a few more capable Croat units on the territory. They posed a different problem. They were better equipped and trained than the village militias, because they had been privately organised by influential or wealthy individuals or by organisations such as HOS, the militia of the Croatian Party of Rights. When Tihomir Blaskic came to the territory, these independent units were not about to give up their independence. Their commanders were strong-willed individuals, like Zuti and Darko Kraljevic. Their men were well-armed, young, fit, and aggressive. They were feared and revered by the local population, including by the village militia units. These pre-existing independent units had their own headquarters. They frequently acted on their own initiative and sometimes helped themselves to the property of others and engaged in other criminal acts. For example, if one of their members was caught committing crimes and was imprisoned, they would go to the Kaonik prison and break out their comrade by force of violence. On other occasions, they attacked other HVO units with which they were displeased. At its peak, the Vitezovi unit had as many as 180 well-armed men. They had been formed after the dissolution of HOS as a special unit responsible directly to the Herceg-Bosna Department of Defence in Mostar. Their salaries came from Mostar and they submitted reports to Mostar. Tihomir Blaskic tried to create a rational, vertical command structure in the operative zone. He gave orders frequently to independent units, such as the Vitezovi, both with respect to operational activities and regarding proper conduct and discipline. We will demonstrate in the Defence case, however, that the Vitezovi did as they pleased. They followed orders from the operative zone when it suited them and did not when they preferred otherwise. These units repeatedly acted on self-initiative, even when contrary to orders from the operative zone. The relationship between the operative zone and these independent units did change over time. By late 1993, when the Vitez-Busovaca enclave was near collapse, all units, militia and independent units, Croat units, that is, paid more attention to the operative zone command, because the lives of everyone in the enclave depended on its success. The evidence will show, however, that that was not the case in the spring of 1993. At that time, discipline within the HVO and independent units was at a very low level, and the ability of the operative zone to control those forces was poor. It is no coincidence that the bulk of the charges in the indictment emanate from events that occurred over three or four days in the middle of April 1993. Those days were a period of intense, chaotic fighting across the Lasva, Kiseljak, and Zenica municipalities. The operative zone headquarters was itself, at times, under direct attack. Information received at the headquarters was incomplete and of poor quality. Command and control over these units was poor at the time of that fighting, just as it was poor when cease-fire agreements were reached and attempts at a high level were made to stop the fighting. Indeed, the evidence will show that time and time again, the top commanders on both sides of the Muslim-Croat war toured the frontlines literally begging local commanders to obey cease-fire orders. The Croats in Central Bosnia did not fare well in the Muslim-Croat war. Vastly outnumbered, they lost extensive territory to the BiH army, including Kakanj, Vares, Fojnica, Travnik, Bugojno, half of Novi Travnik, most of the Busovaca municipality, and much of the Vitez municipality. In January 1993, the BiH army cut the Vitez-Busovaca enclave from the Kiseljak enclave. From the 16th of April forward, the Vitez-Busovaca pocket was physically cut off from the rest of the operative zone, indeed, from the rest of the world and was under siege. The evidence will show that throughout this long siege of the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, Tihomir Blaskic made diligent, and often remarkable, efforts to improve discipline in all HVO units. He ordered soldiers to protect civilians, civilian property, and sacral objects. He ordered criminal elements to be removed from HVO ranks. He ordered that the system of military discipline be used. He even intervened in some individual incidents himself, despite his status as the commander of an operative zone equivalent to a division, to direct more thorough investigation of misconduct and adherence to military discipline. He made these efforts, despite the fact that there was a war raging outside his door with soldiers for whom he was responsible dying every day. Despite his efforts, crimes did occur. Civilians were targeted and killed, particularly in Ahmici on the early morning of the 16th of April, 1993. When the massacre at Ahmici became known, some five or six days later, Blaskic condemned it. He called for an investigation and punishment of those responsible, and he did so publicly. He also ordered an investigation into the massacre, not once, but twice, and also referred it to the HVO main command for further action. After the intense fighting in mid April and that period, the indictment contains very few specific charges in the Lasva Valley over the entire remainder of the war. That is true, despite the fact that the strategic position of the HVO became increasingly desperate as 1993 wore on. Through his continuing efforts to create a more disciplined, responsive, and responsible army, Tihomir Blaskic improved command and control in the HVO which led to fewer and fewer incidents of misconduct. Having voluntarily appeared before this Tribunal in April of 1996, Tihomir Blaskic is pleased to commence here today his defence to the charges against him. In this opening statement, I will outline the evidence that Mr. Nobilo and I will present in our case to Your Honours. I will address the disintegration of Yugoslavia briefly, the formation of the HVO, the deployment of forces in Central Bosnia, conflicts between the HVO and Territorial Defence in 1992, attempts to cut the Kiseljak enclave in both 1992 and 1993. I will discuss command and control specifically within the HVO; the April 1993 conflict, Tihomir Blaskic's response to that conflict, including the Ahmici massacre; and the remainder of the war in the Kiseljak and Lasva Valleys. Finally, I will address the subjects of population movements during the war as well as the evidence on the subject of whether there existed an international armed conflict in the theatre. With your leave, I expect to take the balance of the afternoon in describing our case to you. We intend to present our first witness to you tomorrow morning. Many events of significance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before you continue, do you have a list of the witnesses that you are intending to submit to the Judges, the list of the witnesses? I was talking about submitting it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can submit whatever the Court desires. We provided a list with our first two witnesses on Friday. Is the Court referring to a different list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Prosecution had given the Judges the list of the witnesses that it was going to call, the entire list. I believe that's what it was, Judge Riad, was it not? Do you intend to let us know about how many witnesses you are going to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You'll be able to do that. Very well. I would like to ask you a second question as well: Do you intend to call the accused to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for having interrupted you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President. Thank you. Many events of significance to Central Bosnia were imposed upon it by external forces. Tihomir Blaskic had to react to and cope with these events. The catalyst for many of these crises was the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia. Our first witness tomorrow will address this complex subject. Yugoslavia never existed as a stable democratic state. Efforts to create a unified Yugoslavia repeatedly resulted in violent civil wars. Indeed, Yugoslavia has had the greatest number of conflicts in the 20th century of any European nation. The primary reason for these conflicts has been its multi-nationalism. In Yugoslavia, the Second World War did not end with the defeat of one side or another. Rather, it ceased because of the defeat of the occupying forces. The German collapse was the end of all of the anti-partisan armed forces. But for millions, nationalist consciousness continued to live. The rifles of the Second World War were not discarded but were saved for another day. After World War II, the only forces for the renewal of Yugoslavia were the outside mega-powers and the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. For the next 40 years, the Communists maintained the unity of Yugoslavia through totalitarian rule. It was not the first time Yugoslavia had been held together by external totalitarian force. Following Tito's death, Yugoslavia began the process of disintegration. The disintegration of Yugoslavia also began to pull apart the social fabric of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Muslims, Croats, and Serbs had led relatively segregated lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina, particularly in the rural areas involved in this case. The prospect of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina raised anxieties among all the minorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning their status in the new independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the 1991 elections, the first free elections in over 50 years, voters were polarised along ethnic lines. The same had been true in prior free elections many decades before. The outbreak of war in Slovenia and Croatia in 1991 accelerated the separation of the Muslim and Croat communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These conflicts were the result of policies formulated by Slobodan Milosevic and implemented by the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army. Their effect was to galvanise Bosnian Croats who saw Croatia under attack and in danger of collapse. Many of them went to Croatia and volunteered in the HV, or army of the Republic of Croatia. After the war, they returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina, many of them with their HV uniforms. Many Muslim citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina reacted to the war in Croatia very differently. Frequently their reaction was, "This is not our war." This is referring to the war in Croatia. They did not perceive that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be the next target of the JNA and the Serb militias. This caused suspicion and distrust between the Muslim and Croat communities, and indeed led to the formation of separate Muslim and Croat military organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, albeit for the common purpose of defending Bosnia-Herzegovina against Serb aggression. In 1992, the two communities were still firm allies against the Serbs. These early events are relevant to this case, Your Honours, because they occurred before Tihomir Blaskic arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, indeed before he returned to the former Yugoslavia from Vienna at all. In July 1992 - and now I would like to turn to the formation of the HVO - when Tihomir Blaskic was appointed commander of the operative zone Central Bosnia, the HVO did not exist as an army, as that term is commonly used. The process of creating a competent military organisation without adequate resources and personnel was long and difficult. Indeed, it is a process that continues to this day with respect to Croat (as well former BiH army formations) in today's federal army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Throughout 1992 and into 1993, Tihomir Blaskic was forced to spend a large proportion of his time and energy trying to build a military organisation that would respond to a vertical command structure. This effort was difficult, it was slow, and it met with mixed success. The level of command and control within the HVO evolved over time into a dynamic process. What was the military organisation of which Tihomir Blaskic inherited command in July of 1992? The Territorial Defence, or TO, was a reserve system in the former Yugoslavia which had been designed to resist aggression from either the Soviet Union or NATO forces, principally through arming local populations. The TO and JNA were two components of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia. Into the spring and summer of 1992, TO officials in some locales were still holdovers from the JNA. For this reason, many citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who wished to prepare to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina against the JNA and Bosnia Serb militia, were not willing to join the TO. Simply put, they did not trust those who had held their same positions of authority in the JNA and TO structures. There were both Muslims and Croats who chose not to join the TO; instead, they joined the Patriotic League or the Municipal Staff. Ultimately, the structure of the TO and its lists of eligible conscripts were inherited by the BiH army. By 1992, the TO were subordinated to the BiH army chain of command, and at all relevant times in this case, that was the case in the Lasva and Kiseljak Valleys. TO units in villages were under effective BiH army command. While the BiH army inherited the TO structure, by contrast, the HVO was formed from scratch. When it was proclaimed to exist on the 8th of April, 1992, it existed largely on paper. There were many impediments to the formation of a Bosnian Croat militia. Among the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia, there were few officers with military education who could contribute to this task, and the effort was impaired by a lack of all kinds of resources, such as weapons, uniforms, communications equipment, barracks, or training facilities. Bosnian Croats had started to organise themselves prior to April 1992 when the HVO was proclaimed. The JNA attack on the Republic of Croatia in 1991 had caused a mania among Bosnian Croats who sought to obtain weapons privately by any means possible. When the JNA and Bosnian Serb militias staged attacks on Croatia from BH soil, President Izetbegovic had proclaimed that this was not our war. His pacifist views further agitated Bosnian Croats who did not believe that a pacifist approach would win over the JNA or Bosnian Serb militia. They were proven right; horribly right. In late 1991, Bosnian Croats and Muslims formed Crisis Staffs on the local level. What did Crisis Staffs do? They made lists of volunteers who were willing to fight, to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, and lists of who had weapons. Units were organised on the territorial principle of one village, one unit. Each village elected its own commander. These were typically local politicians. The units were loyal to these local politicians who also provided them with whatever resources were available. These units were focused almost exclusively on local interests and the defence of their local village. This dominance of local interests impeded the creation of a unified militia with a vertical command structure. In April 1992, the inadequacies of the Crisis Staff system led to their replacement with the HVO municipal headquarters and the formation of regional headquarters above the municipal headquarters level. Although the titles had changed, little else had changed in these units. The first action by the HVO militia in Central Bosnia took place on the 6th of May, 1992. They attacked the JNA barracks at Slejmena near Travnik and around 1.500 or so weapons were captured. Two Bosnian Croats were killed. The TO did not participate in that attack, but after it was over, they came to the scene and asked for half of the guns. They took them and then civilians came and took away a large number of damaged weapons. This incident is relevant insofar as it furthered suspicions and mistrust between the two military organisations and communities. Tihomir Blaskic was nominated for the job of commander of the operative zone Central Bosnia because it was thought that the fact that he had left the JNA early in 1991 might engender more trust in him by the people of Central Bosnia than they had in those JNA officers who had extended their stay in the JNA. What did he do when he got the job? When he first came to the Lasva Valley, there were many kilometres of frontlines against the Serbs in the Central Bosnia region. He was responsible for front-line positions against the Serbs in such far-flung places as Jajce, Maglaj, Sarajevo, Kresevo, Bugojno, Zepce, Usora, Travnik, and Novi Travnik. For some time, he would spend 80 per cent of his time organising the defence of these lines and finding soldiers willing to perform a shift at the front-line. Jajce at the time was virtually encircled by the Serbs and was in a precarious position. He visited that town frequently in 1992 and devoted much time to its defence. He also worked hard to try and establish an effective system of command within the HVO militia. He had been trained at military academy and indeed, as a captain in the JNA, had to write proper military orders, and he wrote a lot of them. He wrote good orders. He ordered the municipal headquarters to better organise themselves. In July 1992, he ordered the formation of operative groups within the operative zone which included a large and far-flung geographic area, as I discussed. Tihomir Blaskic saw that the operative zone was hopelessly large and unwieldy, given the transportation and communications difficulties in the theatre. Central Bosnia consists of difficult mountainous terrain. May I approach the relief model, Mr. President? Thank you. These relief models depict the Lasva and Kiseljak Valleys. To my left is the Lasva Valley and to my right is the Kiseljak Valley. The Lasva Valley stretches from my left in Travnik, to Vitez in the centre of this model, and then down the valley to Busovaca. As the Court can see from this model, the Lasva Valley, like all valleys, is a valley surrounded by mountains. This relief map is two-scale, but the height has been magnified by three times to improve readability of topographical variations. During winter, access to this valley is extremely difficult and frequently impossible due to snow and ice and impassable roads. Within the valley is a single spinal road that traverses the valley floor the length of the valley. The Kiseljak Valley is similarly situated. The same spinal road or main supply route, in military terms, continues to run from Busovaca to Kiseljak and on down to this intersection, which is Han Ploca. For orientation purposes, to the east or north-east of Kiseljak is the city of Visoko, and to the west, north-west, is the town of Fojnica. These two models connect at the rough break point around Kacuni, between the Lasva Valley and the Kiseljak Valley. From time to time in our case, Mr. President, we will use these relief models, place markings, flags and the like upon them, and ask that photographs or video stills be made for the record. To try and improve control over militia units, in light of his far-flung responsibilities, in October of 1992, Tihomir Blaskic established four, and later three, operative groups. These operative groups established a level of command between the operative zone command and the municipal headquarters level, what would later become the brigades. We will review that graphically later on in my remarks. At this point, in 1992, there were no HVO brigades. They had not yet been formed. In November of 1992, Tihomir Blaskic took another step to try and organise the HVO militia by forming an operative zone command or zone headquarters and a headquarters staff. He created a well-designed and thought-out plan for the operative zone headquarters, and we will offer it in evidence. The principal problem with this plan was that there were only personnel available to fill one-third of the needed positions, and less than one-half of those personnel who were available had any qualifications for those positions. Their level of education was generally low. Tihomir Blaskic put the operative zone headquarters in Kruscica, a predominantly Muslim area to the immediate north of Vitez. Later, it would have to be moved for reasons that I will discuss. Again in late November 1992, Tihomir Blaskic took further steps to try and form a properly organised and responsive militia. He replaced the system of municipal and regional headquarters with the brigade system. This was the first attempt in the HVO to form brigades. The principal difficulty faced, or one of the difficulties faced in this task, was that formation of brigades challenged the authority and control of local political leaders over the municipal staffs. They would be replaced by brigade commanders. In Vitez, for example, the process of forming a brigade was not completed prior to the April 1993 conflict. The formation of brigades did not alter the relatively low levels of training and discipline among the soldiers themselves. Although most men in the former Yugoslavia had served for one year as JNA conscripts, these conscripts were taught how to shoot a gun and dig a trench, not how to work in an organised military unit, how to organise such units, or how to command such units. The result of the lack of any capable army, either Croat or Muslim, to resist the JNA and Bosnian Serb militia during 1992, was dramatic. By the spring, the JNA and Bosnian Serb militia had overrun two-thirds of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If I could have the first slide, please? These slides, Mr. President, will appear on the computer monitor channel. On this map, marked as "A," the pink areas are those that were controlled by the JNA and Bosnian Serb militia in approximately the spring of 1992. As you can see, roughly two-thirds of Bosnia-Herzegovina is in pink or purple, which was the situation when Tihomir Blaskic came to the Lasva Valley in July of 1992. One can also see from this map that the only resupply routes into Central Bosnia are from the lower left-hand corner of the map through the light blue finger, which is Dalmatia in Croatia, and then through the dark blue mass which constitutes territory the HVO did control in Herzegovina. That was the sole route into Central Bosnia. On this map, the Lasva and Kiseljak Valleys are shown as enclaves not connected which was not yet the case in 1992. If I could have the next slide, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map, this exhibit, is numbered D58.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This map, marked as "E," depicts the areas occupied by a majority of a particular ethnic group in the Central Bosnia area prior to the fall of Jajce in October of 1992. These groupings generally correspond to control by the army or militia units of one party or another. Areas under control of the JNA or Bosnian Serb militia are depicted in brownish red with a red border; areas under Territorial Defence or BiH army control are in green; and Bosnian Croat militia control, blue. You can see from Map E the precarious position of Jajce at this time prior to the 24th of October, 1992. Jajce is virtually encircled and access was limited to the narrow finger which is depicted on the map. This narrow corridor was exposed to Serb fire and could only be used at night. The effort required in the fall of 1992 to sustain the defence of Jajce, which was a joint defence mounted by Muslim and Croat militia forces, exposed the building tensions between the Croat and Muslim militias in Central Bosnia. By October 1992, the Bosnian Croats and Muslims had created two poorly organised military organisations which, as the slide on the video that is Map E depicts, existed on the same territory in Central Bosnia; that is depicted on this map by the fact that blue areas and green areas are completely interspersed and mixed. These two militias, imposed over the same territory, competed for authority and resources. Predictable friction arose and incidents between the soldiers of these two militias proliferated into the fall of 1992. No civil structures existed to adequately address these conflicts. On the contrary, the existence of parallel and duplicative civil structures aggravated the growing tension between the Muslim and Croat communities. In parts of the territory of Central Bosnia, officials of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna established civilian government institutions while in municipalities where it lost the 1991 election, SDA and Muslim authorities established war presidencies with similar and again overlapping responsibilities. Where two government structures and militias exist on the same territory and compete for authority and resources, the evidence will show that conflict between them was virtually inevitable, and conflict there was. In October 1992, open conflict did break out in Novi Travnik between BiH army and HVO soldiers. This conflict arose as a result of a local dispute over the control of a gas station and a hotel. This type of dispute was typical, because of the scarcity of resources and the competing needs of these two militias for petrol, barracks, and the like. When this conflict broke out, Tihomir Blaskic was in Mostar, seeking resupply for the joint Croat-Muslim forces then defending Jajce. The BiH army that was commanded by the 3rd Corps in Zenica, however, was paying closer attention to the local conflict in Novi Travnik than was Tihomir Blaskic. The 3rd Corps ordered that a blockade be established to prevent any HVO troops from the directions of Busovaca or Kiseljak from reaching Novi Travnik. The 3rd Corps ordered that the barricade be established and manned by Territorial Defence soldiers at the point at which the Territorial Defence was strongest along the critical main supply route or spinal road running through the Lasva Valley. Where was that point? If I could have the next slide, please. This map marked as "B" depicts the ethnic composition of the area of Ahmici and surrounding villages, according to the 1991 census. Areas circled in blue depict a Croat majority, while green areas depict a Muslim majority. The black line or brown line, as it may be, running from Dubravica on the left and down to the lower right-hand corner of the map is the main supply route, the Vitez-Busovaca main road. Vitez is to the immediate left of this map, and Busovaca is some distance to the right. Like the HVO militia, units of the Territorial Defence were also territorially based. TO soldiers lived in their village, had their weapons at home, and thus where there was a concentration of Muslim inhabitants in the Lasva or Kiseljak Valleys, there were typically TO or even BiH army units. Such was the case in Ahmici in October of 1992. On the 19th of October, the 3rd Corps command ordered the commander in Ahmici to erect a barricade on the main supply route. They did as they were told. A barricade was erected and was manned by, approximately, 30 soldiers. The barricade was effective, and on the 19th of October, the TO unit in Ahmici captured and disarmed four HVO military policemen who came upon the barricade. Attempts to diffuse the situation were made through local negotiations in Vitez but the barricade remained. By the morning of the 20th of October, the TO soldiers manning the barricade had dug in with fortified positions. Soldiers from the military police, the HVO military police, returned to the barricade on the morning of the 20th of October and attacked the barricade. After several hours, the battle was over and the TO withdrew. Each side sustained one dead in this conflict. But the conflict had spread, further eroding trust and fanning distrust between the Croat and Muslim militias. In Vitez, at this same time, the HVO unit attacked the Territorial Defence headquarters. In Kruscica, the BiH army laid siege to the HVO operative zone headquarters, which you will recall Tihomir Blaskic had placed in a Muslim portion of that town, and demanded that the headquarters staff surrender. By the 22nd of October, 1992, a cease-fire was reached by the local Vitez authorities. What had Tihomir Blaskic been trying to do during this conflict? As I said, he had been trying to organise a convoy of military aid for Jajce and, in fact, was blocked by this very barricade on the main road and prevented from returning to Vitez until after the battle at Ahmici on the 20th of October, 1992. He had gone to both Mostar and Sarajevo to try and put together a convoy for Jajce. But with the conflicts in Novi Travnik and Ahmici, distrust and suspicion were building between the two militias. No relief convoy for Jajce could be organised in this atmosphere. As a result of this conflict, the HVO and the TO in Vitez literally pulled away from each other, and the process of separation continued. The BiH army relocated its headquarters from Vitez into Stari Vitez, and the HVO moved its headquarters from Kruscica to the Hotel Vitez in the centre of Vitez, but the mood had changed in Vitez. The Territorial Defence leadership in Vitez subsequently met and discussed preparations for war against the HVO. Some members of the Territorial Defence resigned, declaring that they were not ready to wage war against the Croats of Vitez. What were the consequences of these conflicts in Jajce? No convoy arrived. There was no resupply. Within four days of the battle in Ahmici, panic broke out in Jajce. 40.000 civilians pulled out. Discouraged and embittered soldiers of both militias, Croat and Muslim, followed. If I could have the next slide, please? This map, denoted "F," depicts the majority ethnic groups and general deployment of forces following the fall of Jajce on the 24th of October, 1992. You will recall on the prior map there was a finger and a circle constituting areas in and around Jajce controlled by green and blue forces. On this map, of course, it is gone, and the people who were in Jajce have all been displaced and expelled into the Lasva Valley. Most of the displaced population was of Muslim ethnicity. There were many Croats as well, but they tended to leave for Croatia, while the Muslims did not. To put these population movements in context, the 40.000 displaced persons from Jajce, compared with a total pre-war population in Vitez of 25.000, by this time, the total number of displaced persons flowing into the Lasva and Kiseljak valleys exceeded 200.000 people. This had more than doubled the existing population of these municipalities. The fall of Jajce and the cumulative influx of displaced persons accelerated the destabilisation of Muslim-Croat relations in Central Bosnia. Already scarce resources, like housing and food, became more so. Displaced Muslim males arriving in Travnik were conscripted into BiH army units, which resulted in a huge imbalance of forces in Travnik between the HVO and the BiH army in favour of the BiH army. There were other implications as well. Displaced Croats and Muslims were angry, frustrated and prone to theft and acts of violence. Some kept their weapons and became uncontrolled. As a result, public security deteriorated in Central Bosnia. In addition, the pre-existing relative balance in ethnic population in the Vitez and Kiseljak municipalities was altered, which contributed to a paranoia among the general Croat population. I would like to elaborate at this point on the issue of maintenance of public order. Tihomir Blaskic neither directed, encouraged, nor acquiesced in the commission of criminal acts against Muslim residents of Vitez or anywhere else. The evidence will show, firstly, that suppression of crime was and continued to be the principal responsibility of civil authorities in Central Bosnia. Tihomir Blaskic was never appointed military governor of that or any other region, nor did he exercise such de facto powers, such as by ruling over civil matters by decree. At all times, civil governments continued to exist in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak, as did the civil police. Where the suspected perpetrator of a criminal act was a civilian or was unknown, investigative jurisdiction lay with the civil police. Where the suspected perpetrator was a member of the HVO, the civil police would refer the matter to the military police for investigation. The ultimate responsibility for initiating prosecution, rendering judgement, and imposing punishment lay with the court system. The evidence will show there was a general breakdown in law and order in the Lasva and Kiseljak valleys as masses of displaced and armed persons arrived in 1992 and 1993. Even large amounts of explosives were commonly available, due to the proximity of the SPS factory outside Vitez, of which we will speak further. The victims of these crimes against property and person were both Muslim and Croat. There was also criminality within HVO ranks. Most soldiers in the militia were on duty for a week or ten days, during which time they were paid as soldiers. The rest of the month they were off duty, civilians, not paid, but still in possession of their uniforms and weapons. Hardships and low morale contributed to alcohol abuse and irresponsible conduct. The civil police worked throughout the war investigating crimes and reporting their results to prosecutors and courts, but their task was difficult. The civil police suffered from a shortage of qualified personnel and equipment. They had no forensic laboratory. The evidence will show that Tihomir Blaskic never interfered with the functioning of the civil police, never told them not to investigate a crime, and never told anyone to give priority to any victim or group of victims of crime. We will present to you investigative records of the civil police to demonstrate their investigation of criminal acts during the war, without regard to the ethnicity of the victim or the perpetrator. What was Tihomir Blaskic's reaction to increases in criminal activity? Yes, Your Honour?

I would suggest to the interpreters that we take a ten-minute break, and then we will take a longer break a little bit later on around 5.00. We will take a ten-minute break now then.
