utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, please turn your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Returning to the subject of public security in Central Bosnia, what was Tihomir Blaskic's response or reaction to the increases in overall levels of crime in Central Bosnia? He took extensive measures to curb criminal acts by HVO soldiers in towns and villages. He repeatedly ordered subordinate commanders to eliminate criminal elements within HVO ranks, to confiscate their uniforms and weapons, to expel them from the HVO, and to use force to prevent them from committing criminal conduct. Now I will turn to events in the Kiseljak municipality in both 1992 and January 1993. In the Kiseljak municipality, as in Vitez, there were both TO and HVO units in most villages. The TO units were not commanded by the 3rd Corps in Zenica. As was the case in the Lasva Valley, they were commanded by the BH command in Visoko to the east of Kiseljak. There were three principal armed conflicts between the Croat and Muslim militias in the Kiseljak municipality, first in August of 1992, then in January of 1993, and then again in April of 1993. Each of these conflicts centred around the same military objective or issue, control over the main supply route or road that runs through the Kiseljak municipality. From the HVO's perspective, it could not defend the Kiseljak Valley if the main supply route was cut. Any portion cut off from Kiseljak proper would be isolated, deprived of reinforcements and resupply, and would collapse if attacked. In August of 1992 and, again, in January 1993, the BiH army took action designed to exert control over the Kiseljak main supply route. The motive was control of this strategic route, as well as control of territory, something that was needed for the large number of Muslim displaced persons driven out of northern and eastern Bosnia by the Serbs. In August 1992, the Territorial Defence in Kiseljak first formed a secret plan to exert control over the Kiseljak main supply route by taking control of the road via military checkpoints at several locations within the Kiseljak municipality. Those locations, which the Territorial Defence forces in Kiseljak intended to establish checkpoints in August of 1992 in order to take control of the main supply route, were located, and I'll point to them, at Bilalovac, which is here, Gomionica, and the village of Gromljak which is across the main supply route from Gomionica. This flag represents Gomionica on the hill above the main supply route. On the other side of Kiseljak, the village of Duhri, D-U-H-R-I, and then finally the village of Han Ploca indicated by the fourth flag of the series I have pointed out, four green flags, that is. The HVO responded to these new checkpoints, and there were fire fights, gun battles, at several of them. The battle at the Duhri checkpoint, which is the third of the four as you go down the road towards Kresevo, was the fiercest and it went on for a number of hours. In the course of this battle, the BH forces fired a weapon from the minaret of the mosque in Duhri. That fire was returned, and the minaret was hit with rounds from an anti-aircraft gun that caused pockmarks to the exterior of the minaret. The damage was minor. When this conflict broke out, Tihomir Blaskic happened to be in Kiseljak. He took action to prevent a wider conflict between the HVO and the TO, he ordered a cease-fire, and he ordered HVO units not to disarm TO units or to issue ultimata to units to disarm. That occurred in August of 1992. The TO attempt to seize control of the main supply route was unsuccessful. The second attempt in January of 1993 by the BH army to cut the main supply route at the northern or north-west end of the Kiseljak enclave, what became an enclave, was successful. Indeed, it is this attempt and this military action that launched the war between Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia that gives rise to the principal charges in this case. The BH attack was consistent with its earlier plan in August of 1992 to exert control over the main supply route in the Kiseljak municipality. The purpose of this attack was simple: to divide and conquer, cut the main supply route, take control of the territory, and connect the BH army forces to the north in Zenica and Visoko with the BH 4th Corps to the south based in Mostar. That was accomplished through this action, as I will describe. At this time, the front-line with the Serbs in Central Bosnia was relatively static. There were few movements in the front-line between the Serbs, on the one hand, and the Croats and Muslims on the other, over the balance of the war in Central Bosnia, from January of 1993 on. The Serb lines were static. Superior Serb weaponry, positions, and forces made territorial gains against the Serbs by the BH army very difficult. By contrast, the Croats were an easier target from which to take territory. Thus, in the third week of January 1993, the BH army established a new checkpoint at this location, Kacuni, which is down the main supply route from Busovaca toward Kiseljak. This checkpoint cut the spinal road connecting the Lasva and Kiseljak Valleys for the rest of the war and the rest of the period covered by this indictment. Fighting, of course, broke out initially at this checkpoint, and in the aftermath, BH army forces from Zenica and from Visoko attacked Croats and Croat villages in a wide swath of territory between Kacuni and Bilalovac which we discussed a moment ago in the context of the August 1992 conflict. Croat villages in between Kacuni and Bilalovac were largely destroyed in the days of fighting after the erection of the roadblock, new checkpoint, at Kacuni. You will hear testimony from witnesses to those attacks, including from the Croat villages of Gusti Grab and Oseliste in this area (indicating). At the same time, this again is January 1993, BH army units attacked a Croat village known as Dusina, which you may recall from earlier testimony. Dusina is located here (indicating) in a small valley over the hill from Busovaca. In the attack on Dusina, more than a dozen civilians and captured soldiers were executed by the BH army soldiers at the scene. You will hear testimony in our case from eyewitnesses to those events. The Dusina killings were the first murders of civilians on the territory of Central Bosnia by either the Croat or Muslim militia, and they served to inflame the situation and the fears and paranoia within the Croat population. Although repeated cease-fires were proclaimed and attempts were made to enforce them, from late January on, the "war within a war," the war between the Muslims and Croats within Central Bosnia encircled by Serbs, had begun. Indeed, these attacks in January of 1993 altered the strategic positions of the warring parties in Central Bosnia. If I could have the next slide, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In order to view the slides, we could perhaps dim the lights a bit because there is a rather unpleasant reflection here. It makes it difficult for all of us to see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This map, labelled as "G," depicts the new deployment of HVO and BH army militia forces following the successful BH army attacks on Kacuni and Bilalovac in January of 1993. Through the Bilalovac-Kacuni breakthrough, the BH army was able to connect the 3rd and 1st Corps in Zenica and Visoko with the 4th Corps to the south. The main supply route from Kiseljak to Busovaca was cut, which is depicted in this map by the continuous area of green between the two blue enclaves which represent the Vitez-Busovaca enclave to the upper or, rather, central portion of the map, as compared to the Kiseljak enclave which appears some distance to the left or the west from Sarajevo. From January 1993 onward, the BH army did not allow the HVO to pass between these two enclaves. This meant that by denying use by the HVO of roads passing through territories to the south and south-west of the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, which the BH army already controlled, they could turn Vitez-Busovaca into an enclave completely encircled by the BH army. And they did. We will introduce evidence in our case concerning what Tihomir Blaskic's role was in this conflict. He had not expected an attack from the BH army in January of 1993. After all, the HVO and the BH army were still allies in the fight against the Serbs. On the 23rd of January, a Saturday, he finished work at his headquarters in Vitez and he went to Brestovsko in the Kiseljak municipality to visit his parents. The BH attacks began on the following day, Sunday, the 24th of January, and on that day, the main supply route was cut. On Monday morning, the next day, he tried to return to the operative zone headquarters in Vitez but the road was cut at Bilalovac. In fact, but for transportation to U.N. meetings in the belly of a BRITBAT Warrior or armoured personnel carrier, he was trapped in Kiseljak until early March 1993 when he was able to return to Vitez, again having been transported there in a U.N. Warrior. On the 27th of January, he met in Kiseljak with UNPROFOR and BiH army representatives. That was three days after the BiH army action had begun. The map marked as "G" depicts the large swath of strategic territory between the two Croat enclaves which had been lost over the prior 72 hours. What was his position at this meeting on the 27th of January? He knew the HVO was hopelessly outnumbered by the BH army 3rd, 1st, and 4th Corps and he had been informed, by the 27th, that the HVO had suffered hundreds of dead and wounded in the conflict over the prior 72 hours. At this meeting on January 27th, he asked for a cease-fire and that the road be unblocked. The BiH army would not open the road, but he nonetheless ordered an unconditional cease-fire to stop the fighting. He had little choice. He continued to pursue peace with the BH army because he knew a larger conflict would be disastrous for the HVO. Two weeks later, on February 13th, at another U.N.-sponsored meeting, Tihomir Blaskic and General Hadzihasanovic issued joint orders for immediate withdrawal of forces to prior positions, assistance to refugees to return to their homes, complete security for the civilian population, unconditional release of all detained persons, removal of all barricades, and free passage for aid and materiel. These are the orders that the U.N. asked for and these are the orders that Tihomir Blaskic issued. He was still isolated in Kiseljak, though, at the time, since the road was never reopened. His ability to influence HVO forces in Busovaca during the late January and March 1993 time period was limited to issuing orders and other directives to them. While in Kiseljak, he received certain reports via an amateur radio software known within the HVO as the "packet radio system." This was the best system the HVO had for sending messages among the Bosnian Croat enclaves in Central Bosnia. When it functioned, the packet radio system enabled the HVO to send short written messages by unsecured radio transmissions. The system, however, was not reliable. These messages were frequently intercepted by the BH army since radio transmissions are open to interception by anyone listening to the right frequency. It also suffered due to a lack of electricity, hardware or software problems, and a lack of trained technical personnel to run the system. In fact, we will introduce documents in our case indicating that on the 26th of January, during the peak of the fighting in the area we have been discussing, only the Vitez packet radio network was operational throughout all of Central Bosnia. What reports did Tihomir Blaskic receive concerning war activity in January and February while he was cut off in Kiseljak? He received a few reports. He was told the BH army had attacked Busovaca, that the villages of Lasva and Dusina were attacked, that other Croat villages had been destroyed, and that HVO casualties were high. In not one of these reports was he given any information relating to any crimes committed by HVO forces in or around Busovaca. The Court will have these reports for its deliberations in this case. Tihomir Blaskic did not wait for the first conflict with the BH army to give explicit directions concerning compliance with the laws of war by the HVO militia. In November of 1992, he warned all HVO unit commanders to prevent soldiers from undertaking illegal actions or other destructive conduct. In response to the violence in Novi Travnik in October, in early November, he directed the HVO in Novi Travnik to take all measures to prevent the burning of Muslim homes in that municipality. In February, he issued an order to all brigades and units to comply with his prior order in January, prohibiting murders, shootings, and bad behaviour, and insisted that subordinate commanders correct such conduct. On the 17th of March, after he returned to the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, he issued a further order to all units to identify members prone to destructive and criminal conduct to remove them from the HVO and confiscate their weapons and uniforms. We will introduce all of these orders into evidence. He took other prophylactic measures. He directed the distribution of calendars to HVO soldiers in both 1992 and 1993 that on one side states the guarantees of the Geneva Convention. It is designed as something that a soldier would carry around in his pocket on a daily basis. On these calendars, soldiers are told that the Conventions require respect and protection for the wounded, the sick, prisoners of war, and civilians. He sent members of every brigade headquarters staff to seminars on the Geneva Conventions and directed that they issue appropriate instructions to their units. When the conflict intensified in April 1993, he issued many additional orders for the protection of civilians and property and compliance with the laws of war, and he repeated those orders even during the most difficult of times for the HVO during the war. We will authenticate these orders through live witness testimony. When compared to orders already in evidence, they will also be shown to be authentic based upon their form, stamps, seals, signatures and other markings. The evidence will show that these orders were issued sincerely and in good faith by Tihomir Blaskic and that he expected them to be carried out by subordinate commanders and by soldiers in the field. Command and control begins with an order but does not end there. The evidence will show that Tihomir Blaskic's orders were not uniformly implemented and obeyed, nor were events in the field always accurately reported to him. We will present evidence in our case concerning what elements are required for effective command and control over military forces and which of those elements did not exist with respect to particular HVO units and time periods. Effective command and control of subordinate units requires a number of elements. Next slide, please. There is a hard copy or paper copy of this slide which each of Your Honours and the members of the Prosecution should have if this is too difficult to read on the screen. The left consists of bullet points in English; the right, of course, French. I will read them. A commander must have the authority to issue commands to the unit in question. A commander must have an effective staff. An order must be effectively communicated to the unit. An order to act must be acted upon promptly by the unit. The subordinate unit must possess an effective organisation enabling responsibilities arising out of an order to act to be properly assigned and carried out. The unit must act consistent with the order. Accurate reports must be promptly relayed up the chain of command. Lastly, acts cannot be taken on self-initiative. At certain times, these preconditions for command and control did not exist within the HVO. We will introduce testimony concerning the HVO brigade in Sarajevo which had almost no ability to communicate with the accused even though the accused was, on paper, responsible for that brigade. After April, when Kiseljak was cut off and the BH army enforced that isolation of the Kiseljak enclave, the HVO in Vitez, the evidence will show, had virtually no control over the HVO in Kiseljak, Fojnica, Vares, or Kakanj, and I will elaborate later in my comments on this issue. This lack of command and control, however, was not the fault of Tihomir Blaskic. He took extensive measures to try and establish an effective system for issuing orders down and for passing reports up the chain of command. His orders regularly assigned personal responsibility for their implementation and demanded a prompt reporting on the actions required by the order. There was, however, a basic shortage of trained or even educated persons in the HVO militia to serve as officers and commanders. What were the consequences? If we could have the next slide, please? This chart, Your Honours, is available in three forms. It's on the video. You also have a small, hard copy of it in the set of materials you've been provided with, and it also exists to my left in large format, shall we say. This chart depicts the levels of command which existed in the operative zone for Central Bosnia. These levels begin, for our purposes, with the commander of the operative zone. That was Tihomir Blaskic. Going down from him, the subordinate levels of command were the operative groups, the brigades, this, of course, was after the brigades were formed, battalion, company, platoon, squad, and fighting group, the most basic element of a fighting force. Roughly, the number of people in these units is depicted to the right of the categories themselves. What else does this chart depict? The left-hand side of the chart depicts the need for orders to be issued by each subordinate commander down to the level of the actual fighting man or soldier in the fighting group. The orders issued at each of these levels must vary somewhat, in that lower level units will be concerned with smaller, more specific tasks, but they must also remain true to the top commander's general instructions for command and control to exist. This process of issuing orders and suborders down to the level of the soldier in the field requires educated persons to function properly. There was a general shortage of educated persons in the Bosnian Croat militia that could perform this task. In fact, most of the HVO brigades either had no officers with formal military education or one or two at the most. That compares to a NATO standard that would require at least 25 times as many trained officers for units of comparable size. Even commanders at a fairly high level in the HVO militia, such as at the brigade level, lacked military education. One brigade commander had been an automobile mechanic before the war. There's nothing wrong with that. It's a profession that many of us come to need at one time or another, but that does not constitute a military training. Another commander of a significant sized unit sold life insurance up until the middle of the war. Effective command and control also requires that the commander receive timely and accurate reports of events in the field. If a commander doesn't know what is happening in the field, he cannot issue effective orders to direct and control those events. Effective reporting, and I'm now indicating to the right-hand side of the chart which has an arrow going up the chain of command back to the commander, effective reporting up the chain of command requires that reports initially made at the level of command, at the level of command at which the reportable event was observed -- the question there, of course, is at what level did the event occur? Did it occur at the level of a platoon, at a company, or at some higher level? Effective reporting requires that the reports be accurate and that the reports actually go up the chain. A report that doesn't reach the commander is a report that, from the perspective of the commander, does not exist. The right-hand portion of the chart indicates, again, the same levels of command but this time the levels of command through which reports must flow in order to reach the commander. The evidence in the case will show that, at critical times, reports either were not made of criminal acts by HVO militia members, or they were made but not accurately reported up the chain of command to Tihomir Blaskic. Both are required for command and control, accurate reporting up and accurate issuance and repetition of orders down the chain of command. Command and control in the operative zone was also undermined by a degree of chaos at the higher level above the commander of the operative zone, off this chart, in other words, above it. At three different times, Tihomir Blaskic was placed under a joint command. That is, he was made subordinate to a joint command comprised of various former HOS and current HVO or BH army commanders. In November 1992, he was ordered to subordinate to a joint command comprised of the former HOS leader Ante Prkacin, as well as Arif Pasalic of the BH army. That changed two months later when he was told to form a joint command with General Hadzihasanovic. In April, he was ordered to form a different joint command, again with the BH army, which proved very difficult, since the two parties were effectively at war during this period. The Defence is not criticising these attempts at peacemaking, nor criticising the idea of joint commands, but the evidence will show that these constantly changing patterns of subordination and responsibility introduced an element of chaos, even at the highest level of command and control in the theatre. Now I will turn to the resumption of the war in April of 1993. After the January war, Tihomir Blaskic found himself in a highly vulnerable military position. With the Vitez-Busovaca-Kiseljak region cut into two separate enclaves, the ability to defend itself against the overwhelming numerical superiority of the BH forces was reduced. Communications and resupply for the Vitez-Busovaca enclave was precarious. Nonetheless, he continued to pursue a course of reconciliation with the BH army following the January war. He knew that confrontation would be disastrous for the HVO. What did he do? In March 1993, he approved the provision of over 6.000 kilograms of explosives to the BH army logistics base in Visoko. On the 1st of April, the 3rd Corps received, through HVO territory, a significant shipment of weapons, including some 15 RPG launchers, 1.500 RPG grenades, and some 150.000 rounds of ammunition. The BH army was preparing for something. Where were the BH army forces in the Lasva Valley? On the 20th of June, 1992, President Izetbegovic had declared a general mobilisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina of all men between the ages of 18 and 65 and all women between the ages of 18 and 55. The entire adult population, in other words, was ordered to report to the nearest TO or Territorial Defence unit. The 3rd Corps, as I have said, commanded the BH army and TO units in the Lasva Valley. There were four brigades in Zenica, three or more in Travnik, including the 7th Muslim Brigade, as well as brigades in Novi Travnik, Busovaca, and Vitez. These are all BH army forces. The BH army brigade in Vitez, known as the 325th Mountain Brigade, was present at battalion strength in Stari Vitez, Kruscica, Preocica, and Poculica. Subordinate companies were located in Bila, Vrhovine, Ahmici, and Vranska, and there were other platoons. The company in Ahmici was part of the battalion located in Preocica. The Ahmici company had a headquarters in the primary school, a radio station, and a centralised stockpile of weapons. The BH army had an interest in taking Vitez. The SPS factory, one of the largest explosives and munitions factories in the former Yugoslavia was a principal target of the BH army. They desperately wanted to control this factory on the outskirts of Vitez. In subsequent international negotiations, President Izetbegovic would demand BH army control of Vitez for this stated reason. As in January, pressure was building to take more territory from the HVO to accommodate displaced persons. April of 1993 saw a resumption of more direct violence, including violence directed against the HVO. On the 8th of April, Easter Sunday, violence broke out in Travnik over the display of Croatian flags, as well as Bosnian flags, on certain buildings. There were both Muslim and Croat casualties as a result. On the 12th of April, several HVO members were stopped in Stari Vitez, interrogated, and beaten. On the 13th of April, four officers of the HVO in Novi Travnik and Travnik were kidnapped. On the 14th of April, an assassination attempt was made of Darko Kraljevic, commander of the independent Vitezovi unit. As the Court has already heard, on the 15th of April, in Zenica, the HVO brigade commander, Zivko Totic, was kidnapped and four HVO soldiers murdered, as was a bystander. This was followed, on the 15th of April, by a complete blockade of Zenica by BH army forces. We will also introduce evidence in our case that on the 15th of April, again, not on the 16th when the general conflict broke out, but the prior day, the 15th of April, 1993, conflict broke out on the strategic location known as Kuber Mountain, K-U-B-E-R. This green flag depicts the highest peak on Kuber Mountain. Kuber Mountain was the dominant feature between the Lasva Valley and Zenica. Zenica was the site of the 3rd Corps and, approximately, 20.000 to 40.000 soldiers in that corps. Exact numbers are not known. Control of Kuber was a critical issue in the control of the Lasva Valley. Prior to the 16th of April, the HVO controlled mountain-top positions on Kuber, but on the 15th, fighting broke out between BH army and HVO positions on Kuber. By 6.00 p.m. on the 15th, reports were made of HVO casualties as a result of that fighting, and those reports had been received by Tihomir Blaskic in the operative zone headquarters. Suffice it to say that by the 15th of April, the HVO and the Lasva Valley was under attack, although principally through attacks on its leadership. Had it come under a direct attack from the BH army and Zenica at the time, the HVO would not, from its existing positions, have been able to defend Vitez. An attack would likely have cut the Vitez-Busovaca pocket and led to the fall of the HVO in that pocket. Had it been divided into multiple, smaller pockets, the HVO forces would not have been able to move and concentrate defensive forces. The main supply route or road served that critical function of enabling them to move and concentrate forces on defensive forces in the case of a BH army attack. In addition, the proximity of Territorial Defence forces to the main supply route, as in Ahmici but at other points in the enclave as well, put HVO control of the main supply route in jeopardy. The October '92 barricade at Ahmici had demonstrated as much. BH army forces within the pocket were also of concern to the HVO. Namely, forces in Kruscica and Stari Vitez could launch mortar, sniper, and even infantry attacks within the Vitez-Busovaca enclave. Also of concern were smaller HVO units in Gacice and Donji Verceriska, which were on dominant hill positions over the SPS factory to the immediate west of Vitez. This was the deteriorating military situation in which Tihomir Blaskic found himself responsible for on the 15th of April, 1993. He had also received two intelligence reports in the previous weeks. We will introduce those reports into evidence. In mid March, he was told to expect a likely BH army attack on Vitez from the direction of Zenica. He was told to expect this likely attack from Zenica towards Vitez with BH army forces coming through Vrhovine, which is right here above the hill from Ahmici, for the purpose, he was told in this intelligence report, of linking up with BH forces which already existed in Vranska, where I'm now pointing, which is on the other side of the main supply route or main road. Were BH forces to link up between Vrhovine, Ahmici, and Vranska, of course, the Vitez-Busovaca pocket would have been cut in half. Towards the end of March, he received a second intelligence report, which we will also offer into evidence, which predicted an attack by the BH army in an attempt to link Zenica, here, with Travnik to the west. The report told him that the attack would likely come from Preocica, which is located here, there's no flag currently at Preocica, but also from Poculica, which is here, and down the hill to Sivrino Selo, a position held by the BH army throughout the war and, literally, within a stone's throw of the main supply route running through the Vitez-Busovaca enclave. In light of these assessments and the escalating attacks on the HVO leadership, as well as the blockade of Zenica on the 15th, Tihomir Blaskic concluded that he had to take steps to prepare to defend Vitez against a possible BH army attack. What did he do? We will prove exactly what he did through his written instructions to HVO forces on the 15th and 16th of April. On the 15th of April at 10.00 in the morning, he issued a written order to all HVO units. First, he set forth his assessment that the BH army would likely attack Kuber Mountain - in fact, that attack happened later in the day, as I've already said - in an attempt to link up with BH forces to the west in Poculica and then across the main supply route in Vranska, which I indicated on the relief model a moment ago. He gave specific and clear assignments in this order. He directed the 4th battalion of the regional military police of the HVO to secure the headquarters of the operative zone and to keep the Busovaca-Vitez-Travnik road open. If any barricades were placed on that road, as had occurred in October of '92, he instructed them to prevent barricades from being placed. Then he gave the critical, for our purposes, instruction. If I could have the next slide, please? Could we, perhaps, zoom in on that slide slightly to make it more legible, or focus, one or the other. No, not possible? Thank you. This is a portion of the order of 15 April at 1000 hours, and I quote: "In the event of a rather strong attack by the Muslim extremist forces from the direction of Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo or Pirici, report to me, and if they shoot directly on you, return fire and neutralise the attacker." To the Vitezovi independent unit in this same order, he gave them the task -- that part of the order is not depicted in this slide, but we will offer this order into evidence in its entirety. To the Vitezovi unit, he gave them the task of responding to any breakthrough by the BH army through the front-line positions of the HVO, particularly in case of an attack from within Stari Vitez towards the Hotel Vitez HVO headquarters. The Vitezovi were directed to block any such attack and protect the headquarters. To all other brigades, he directed a state of preparedness to carry out a defence of their zone of responsibility. He instructed the HVO brigades, in case of an attack, to withdraw only after evacuating the population and with his consent. In this order on the 15th, he spoke of the possible need to withdraw in the face of the BH army attack he was expecting. None of these units were ordered to attack the BH army, much less any civilians or civilian objects. At 15.45, he issued a second order, on the 15th of April. This order went to the HVO in Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Zenica, Travnik, and Novi Travnik. In it, he outlined the continuing threat to the HVO leadership from possible terrorist attacks, attempts to liquidate the leadership, and he ordered these units to prepare small groups to defend against possible further terrorist attacks on HVO commanders. On the 16th, he issued one more order at 1.30 a.m. So the night of the 15th, early morning hours of the 16th, he issued a further combat order to the Vitez brigade and the Tvrtko special unit. They were ordered to stop the attack of the BH army and block BH army forces in Kruscica, Vranska, which I indicated a moment ago, and Donji Vecerska, one of the villages adjacent to the SPS factory. He explained in the order that an attack by the enemy was expected from the direction of the south, Kruscica and Vranska, and that the duty of the units addressed was to block these villages and to stop movement in and out. He directed that "If the enemy attacks you openly, stop his movement." All three of these orders were defensive. None of them directed an attack; only to respond if attacked. None of them directed an attack on civilians. None of them singled out Ahmici for any military action. No such order was given by Tihomir Blaskic on the 15th of April or at any other time. On the morning -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we're going to take a 20-minute break. All right. We will suspend the hearing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Please have the accused brought in. Mr. Hayman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I described the orders, combat orders, given by Tihomir Blaskic on the 15th and early morning of the 16th of April. What happened on the morning of the 16th of April? Clearly, fighting broke out between the Muslim and Croat militias in the Lasva Valley. Who fired the first shots is not particularly relevant to this case. What is clear is that forces of both the HVO and the BH army were in close proximity to each other in several locations, and fighting between them spread across the greater Vitez area on the morning of the 16th. Before continuing on with the events of that day, I would like to briefly return to the issue of the HVO command structure. The orders I mentioned before the break included orders to HVO brigades, the 4th Battalion of the regional military police, and the Vitezovi independent unit. What was Blaskic's command relationship to these units? This is a central issue for command responsibility. If I could have the next slide, please? This slide also, Your Honours, will exist on the video. You have a small printed version in the materials that you should have, and it also has been replicated in large format to my left. This chart depicts the organisation of the HVO military in the Central Bosnia operative zone and its larger context, the framework within which the central zone of the HVO, the operative zone, existed. Across the top of the chart are the various departments of the HVO civil structure within Herceg-Bosna. So you have, for example, the Department of Social Activities, Department of Commerce, Department of Internal Affairs, Department of Finance, and Department of Justice. Normal types of civil governmental bureaux or departments. The department of interest, for our purposes, is the Department of Defence, which is depicted in the middle of the top line of the chart. There are three elements within the Department of Defence that are relevant again for our purposes, and they are depicted -- well, there are actually four. There are three at one level and then there is a fourth that is depicted at a lower level to the right of the chart because of space limitations. What are they? In the centre, there are the headquarters of the HVO. That is a reference to the main headquarters of the HVO in Mostar, subordinate to the Department of Defence. But there were other elements on the same level as the HVO military headquarters. What were they? To the left, we see the head office for military police. That was a separate office within the Department of Defence that was not under the HVO headquarters. In addition, to the right, we have the head office for Security Information Service. That is not a unit, that is a service. It is an internal security service, if you will, that existed again as a service or bureau within the Department of Defence and was not subordinate to the HVO headquarters. Fourthly, following the line to the right and down, there are three special purpose units with a direct line of command to the Department of Defence. They were the Vitezovi unit, the Busic unit, and the Pavlovic or Ludwig Pavlovic unit. They are depicted to the right of the chart. Under the HVO military headquarters, the main staff, there are three operative zones not depicted at the same level here simply because of space limitations. You have the first operative zone and the second operative zone, but at the same level, the third operative zone, which has been dropped down one level in order to provide more space to depict other relationships. The third operative zone was the operative zone for Central Bosnia. That is the zone, of course, we are concerned about in this case for the most part. Underneath the third operative zone, with a direct line or chain of command, were the various brigades and units that were directly subordinated to the operative zone for Central Bosnia. By way of explanation, some of these are instantly recognisable, such as the Vitez brigade and the Travnik brigade. These other brigades, in short, the Ban Jelacic Brigade was in Kiseljak, the Stjepan Tomasevic brigade was in Novi Travnik, the Bobovac brigade was in Vares, the 111xp brigade was in Zepce, the King Tvrtko brigade was in Sarajevo, and the Kontromanic brigade was in Kakanj. I think I covered them. The anti-aircraft defence unit was a central unit for all anti-aircraft weapons, while the light artillery and rocket division was a small unit with all other artillery pieces centralised in that unit. Not on this chart at this level for space reasons are the HVO brigades in Zenica and Travnik which fell in 1993 or the HVO brigade in Usora some distance to the north of the Lasva Valley. Now, of importance for the Defence case and the matters about which we will be admitting specific evidence relate to the three entities which exist on the same level as the operative zone for Central Bosnia and that are connected with the operative zone by dotted lines. You see a dotted line here, dotted line here, and another dotted line going over to the Vitezovi unit (indicating). These dotted lines reflect the fact that each of these units, in the case of the military police and the Vitezovi and the Service, the Security and Information Service, were required, under the scheme which was in force, to coordinate and assist the operative zone command on an as-needed basis, when in the theatre. When in the area of responsibility, they had, on paper, a responsibility to coordinate with the operative zone. At the same time, their principal command lines lay elsewhere. The 4th Battalion of the regional military police had a direct line of command to the head office for military police in Mostar; the SIS in Central Bosnia had a direct line of responsibility to the head office for SIS; and the Vitezovi special purpose unit, like the other special purpose units, had a direct line of responsibility to the Department of Defence. Thus, over each of those three -- those two units and that one service -- there were dual lines, if you will, of command over them, and the operative zone for Central Bosnia did not have, even on paper, an exclusive command relationship with those entities. Now I will return to the 16th of April. The orders given to units in the Vitez area thus were to block enemy forces, to secure the road, and to return fire only if directly fired upon. The evidence will show that these orders were not uniformly implemented; rather, very different actions were pursued in different locations based upon the same orders from the operative zone headquarters. I will review each geographic location of interest. First, Stari Vitez. Fire was exchanged between the HVO and the Territorial Defence units in Stari Vitez on the morning of the 16th of April. There were approximately 250 BH soldiers in Stari Vitez. As a result of this fighting, neither side gained any appreciable territory. Houses and other structures, rather than trenches, were used by both militias in this fight, and houses of both Croats and Muslims were burned and destroyed as a result of that fighting. Other Muslim houses, near what has been referred to as the "Yellow Building," also appear to have been looted and burned intentionally and not as a result of combat activity. This was the area in which the Vitezovi soldiers operated and were active, and although their activities were limited to a small number of houses, they were directly contrary to the orders of Tihomir Blaskic. Although he did not order an attack on Stari Vitez - he ordered that the BH army be blocked in Stari Vitez - the BH army presence in Stari Vitez nonetheless had military significance to the HVO. It was defended by the BH army, indeed successfully defended with significant casualties inflicted on the HVO forces engaged. Over the course of the 16th of April, HVO soldiers were killed and wounded in exchanges with the BH army around the edges of Stari Vitez. Now I will turn to Kruscica. A battle also occurred in Kruscica on the 16th of April. Tihomir Blaskic gave the same orders relating to Kruscica as he did to other locations such as Donji Vecerska, yet no specific crime is alleged in the indictment to have resulted in Kruscica. Kruscica was defended by the BH army, the defence was organised, and it was successful. Kruscica was never taken by the HVO during the balance of the war. What happened in Donji Vecerska? Donji Vecerska was defended by a unit of the Territorial Defence. The village had a plan of defence, and with automatic weapons, sub-machine guns, and a heavy machine gun, implemented that plan of defence. There were approximately 750 Muslim residents in that village. The battle between the HVO and Territorial Defence units there lasted all day on the 16th of April, all day on the 17th, and lasted until midday on the 18th. Then the TO units withdrew from the village. Despite the fact that the fighting in that village went on for two and a half days, a total of eight Muslim soldiers and civilians were wounded or killed out of the more than 700 present; approximately nine Croats were wounded and one killed. The indictment does not specifically charge an unlawful attack on civilians or civilian objects in Donji Vecerska on the 16 of April; rather, it is identified as a location in which the unlawful destruction or plunder of property occurred. As the front-line in the village moved around during this two-and-a-half-day fight, houses were burned, both Croat and Muslim. It appears neighbours could see each other burning the other's houses, and a process of reaction and retaliation followed. The evidence will show that the characteristics, the local characteristics of that three-day battle and the property that was destroyed during that time, was a function of local events. The characteristics of the battle was a function of local events and not the orders of the operative zone commander. Poculica is another location which is not specifically named as the site of any offences in the indictment. Poculica is located here, there is a green flag indicating it, and it is on the road from Vitez to Zenica. It lies above the hillside which contains Nadioci, Ahmici, Pirici, Santici, Sivrino Selo. On the morning of the 16th of April in Poculica, what happened? It was a mixed village of Muslims and Croats, more Muslims than Croats, and on the morning of the 16th, the Territorial Defence unit in Poculica attacked the Croat part of the village. Hundreds of Croats fled into a stream to try and escape down the hill, and approximately 70 did not flee and they were captured by the Territorial Defence forces in Poculica. In the following days, regrettably, those detainees were taken in groups to dig trenches, some were forced to go out into no man's land to collect bodies while tethered to a rope which their captors held onto, and indeed a number of them were murdered and wounded by a shooting incident involving a BH soldier. Some but not all of these 70 detainees were exchanged on the 1st of May. Evidence concerning what happened in Poculica will not be introduced to suggest that one crime justifies another. It does not. Let me make that perfectly clear. Nonetheless, what happened in Poculica, beginning on the morning of the 16th of April, is relevant to whether, on that day, there were attacks on Croats and Croat forces in the Lasva Valley and whether such attacks and the fact of them were actually reported to the Hotel Vitez where Tihomir Blaskic was such that that information shaped his perception of the events of that day and affected his responses to events and to that information. Gacice is another village near Vitez which overlooks the SPS factory from a hill feature. There is no unlawful attack on civilians in Gacice charged in the indictment. The only specific charge is unlawful destruction or plunder of property. In Gacice, there was a Territorial Defence unit of some 50 or 60 soldiers, and on the 16th of April, the Muslim and Croat militias in Gacice gathered and squared off but they did not fight. For three days, they negotiated over surrender of weapons, and both sides dug trenches. By the 20th of April, these discussions had collapsed, and the Vitezovi unit went to Gacice and participated in an attack on the Territorial Defence units in Gacice. In this conflict, there were five men killed, one Croat and four Muslim. In the lower part of the village, the Territorial Defence unit surrendered along with weapons, explosives, and the like which they possessed, and in the upper part of the village, the Territorial Defence soldiers withdrew into BH army territory. In the course of this battle, it appears one Vitezovi soldier was killed. A number of houses appeared to have been burned down in retaliation for the death of that Vitezovi soldier. This is a pattern, which the Court will see from the evidence, was repeated at many different times in many different places; namely, in both the HVO and BH militias, a lack of discipline and control within units caused, where a soldier was killed, immediate retaliation by the soldier's comrades, colleagues - call them what you will - against civilians or civilian objects. This happened not only in Gacice, it happened in Rotilj, which I will discuss later in my comments, it happened in Miletici, where four Croats were executed in direct retaliation for the death of a Mujahedin fighter. Now I will turn to the villages or hamlets more properly known as Nadioci, Ahmici, Pirici, and Santici. These villages or hamlets are all located within a kilometre or two of each other. They are one small area off of the main supply route which runs through the Vitez-Busovaca area. I wanted to call the Court's attention to the fact that they are all located in very, very close proximity to each other. We will introduce evidence in our case concerning the nature of the organised defence that was being prepared in Ahmici prior to the conflict. Although Tihomir Blaskic did not order an attack on Ahmici, it is still relevant that there was an organised defence and that there was a significant battle there on the 16th. It is certainly relevant to subsequent reports he received and information he received. On the 11th of April, a meeting of the Ahmici Territorial Defence unit was held, at which a plan of defence was discussed and a front-line identified in the case of any attack. On the 15th of April, the Territorial Defence unit in Ahmici observed Croats gathering in the village and at 8.00 p.m. convened a meeting. They reviewed their lines of defence and ammunition, including rocket-propelled grenades, was distributed to certain members of the unit. As I said earlier, the order from Tihomir Blaskic concerning this region directed the military police to secure the main supply route and, in case of attack, notify him, and only then should fire be returned against the attackers. There was significant and organised resistance in Ahmici on the 16th of April. Exactly how that fight began is a question that I cannot tell you we will answer specifically in our case. The fighting between military units in Ahmici went all day on the 16th, and casualties were sustained among the military police that were present. Nonetheless, what is clear and what the evidence in our case will make clear is that Tihomir Blaskic's orders were not followed in Ahmici. Civilians in Ahmici were intentionally targeted and killed. All Muslim homes in Ahmici were burned. These actions were not pursuant to any order from Tihomir Blaskic. They were contrary to his express written orders. The sacking of Ahmici occurred without his knowledge and in the absence of his receipt of any information suggesting that a massacre was to occur or would occur in Ahmici. The massacre was over within a matter of hours, by midday, if not late morning, on the 16th. The fighting between military units apparently continued until nightfall when the TO unit evacuated to Vrhovine above the village. We will present direct evidence in our case concerning what information Tihomir Blaskic received concerning the combat activities that occurred on the 16th of April, 1993. On the morning of the 16th, he awoke to a general conflict in the Vitez municipality between HVO and BH army militia units. Shells were falling in Vitez, and the Hotel Vitez was under sniper fire from Stari Vitez. He moved the headquarters operations room into the basement of the hotel for security, but from the basement, no direct observations could be made about what was occurring in the area. The HVO had no armoured vehicles for secure transportation, and he, necessarily, spent the day in the basement of the Hotel Vitez. He asked for regular reports so he could inform himself what was occurring in the field. What reports did he receive? We will introduce those reports into evidence. At 7.00 in the morning, the Vitez brigade reported that most of the headquarters staff could not make it to the brigade headquarters and that the situation at headquarters was chaotic. That was a written report. At 9.00 in the morning, the Vitez brigade further reported that there were mortar attacks against Vitez, that there was infantry fighting in Stari Vitez and from Kruscica, and that Croats in Poculica were calling, that they were under attack and asking what to do. The HVO in Busovaca reported that at 6.30 a.m. on the 16th, the BH army launched attacks from Gornji Rovna, Pezici, and Bare, and in defending these attacks, the HVO, on the 16th, had sustained three dead, nine wounded and two missing. It was through these and similar reports that Tihomir Blaskic gained what information he could concerning the day's events. The true events that day in Ahmici were never reported to him by the military policemen present in the village. The unlawful burning of houses in other locations of the Vitez municipality were, likewise, not reported to him. What was his reaction to this general conflagration on the 16th? First, he tried to stop the fighting. At 10.00, he directed that BRITBAT be contacted to assist in trying to arrange a cease-fire. The phone in the hotel did not work, so he sent a messenger. A meeting was arranged with warrior transport from the U.N., and he sent two members of his headquarters staff to the meeting. Although no representative from the 3rd Corps came, the HVO agreed to a cease-fire. And at 1600 hours on the 16th, Tihomir Blaskic ordered an immediate and unconditional cease-fire to HVO units. Also on the morning of the 16th, he tried to obtain a cease-fire through another channel. He tried to contact Alija Izetbegovic through an intermediary, a religious authority, in order to stop the fighting. He wanted to stop it because he knew a general conflict between the HVO and the BH army would be a disaster for the HVO and Croats in Central Bosnia. But the cease-fire did not hold, and the BH army immediately went on the attack. He continued to seek a cease-fire on the 17th of April and on the 18th of April, when another cease-fire agreement was reached. He also tried to better secure the defence of the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, and his orders reflect that desire. On the evening of the 16th, he ordered the Zenica brigade to try and stop the advance of BH army forces from Zenica towards Vitez. He ordered a unit of the military police in Travnik to relocate to Vitez to provide reinforcements. At 4.00 in the morning on the 17th of April, he ordered the Busovaca and Vitez brigades to defend against expected continuing BH army attacks. In this order, less than 24 hours after the general conflict on the morning of the 16th began, he specifically instructed the commanders of the Busovaca and Vitez brigades as follows. Next slide, please, and I quote from that order: "Soldiers are to be specifically cautioned about how to treat civilians, the elderly, women and children, who are not to be killed because that is a crime." In his original order he wrote "crime" in all caps for emphasis. We will introduce that order into evidence. As the 16th wore on, the BH army broadened its attacks against HVO positions. At noon on the 16th, BH army units were ordered to attack the HVO in the Jelinak-Loncari area for the purpose of advancing to the main supply route just west of Busovaca and cutting that main supply route. Those units did launch that attack, and on the 17th, the HVO position continued to deteriorate. The attack, as I described, on Kuber and Jelinak occurred. An HVO unit was also cut off and surrounded in Kruscica, and so forth. On the night of the 17th to the 18th of April, Tihomir Blaskic ordered the Kiseljak brigade to try and take action to block BH army forces in villages, specifically Visnjica and other villages from which attacks were possible, and he ordered the Kiseljak brigade to try and capture Gomionica and Svinjarevo, where large numbers of BH troops were located. Gomionica, you may recall, was the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in the Kiseljak municipality, and the evidence will show it was well defended by 200 or more BH army soldiers. It also had strategic significance, which I'd like to indicate to you. Gomionica, which is located roughly at this green flag, is on the main supply route that runs through the Kiseljak Valley. From the Territorial Defence headquarters in Gomionica to territory controlled by the BH army based in Fojnica was a relatively short distance to that territory. Heading in the other direction, the Territorial Defence units in Gomionica controlled territory contiguous to that controlled by the BH army based in Visoko. So this point, the Gomionica-Svinjarevo point in the Kiseljak enclave, is the narrowest and was the narrowest point of the enclave and was a logical point at which the BH army might try and cut the enclave, as, indeed, had occurred. On the 18th of April, there was a military conflict in Gomionica, and it went on for a long period of time. In lower Gomionica, the fight went on for days, and after the Territorial Defence and BH army units retreated up the hill to upper Gomionica, they were there for weeks and weeks. And, in fact, the fighting went on for a period of weeks. Tihomir Blaskic's orders to the Kiseljak brigade to take action against that Territorial Defence stronghold are military, strictly military, orders. Indeed, there are no specific allegations of attacks on civilians in Gomionica. Tihomir Blaskic received no reports of improper conduct or war activities in that area, and, indeed, he could not visit that area during this period of time, because he was cut-off in the Vitez-Busovaca enclave. During the day on the 18th of April, Mate Boban and President Izetbegovic met in Zagreb. They agreed to another cease-fire. That cease-fire was ordered by General Petkovic and ordered by Tihomir Blaskic on the afternoon of the 18th, but that cease-fire also did not hold. By the end of the day, the operative zone headquarters received reports that the HVO brigade in Zenica was still under attack, and the Kiseljak HVO reported that fighting was ongoing in Rotilj, Visnjica, Doci, Hercezi, and Brestovsko. They reported heavy fighting in Gomionica. Nor did a cease-fire hold on the following day, the 19th. On the 20th, there was a peace conference in Zenica, at which Tihomir Blaskic attended, and another cease-fire was agreed upon which he ordered be implemented. Much of the case we have listened to over the past year relates to the massacre in Ahmici on the 16th of April. In the Defence case, we will introduce evidence concerning when Tihomir Blaskic learned there had been a massacre in Ahmici and what his response was. During the period from the 16th to the 20th of April, there were no reports to him of a massacre in Ahmici. The British battalion was located a few kilometres down the road from the Hotel Vitez. They had regular warrior patrols during the conflict in Ahmici. When did they discover the proportions of the massacre in Ahmici? Not until the 22nd of April, six days after the event. Shortly after the discovery, Colonel Stewart of the British battalion visited Tihomir Blaskic and impressed upon him the gravity of the crimes in Ahmici. Colonel Stewart at this meeting found that Blaskic was, and I quote, "absolutely horrified at what took place in Ahmici." In a follow-up letter, Colonel Stewart requested Tihomir Blaskic's help in investigating the sacking of Ahmici. Tihomir Blaskic was surprised by what he had been told. He had received no reports within the HVO of any killing of civilians in Ahmici. What did he do? Within 48 hours of the 22nd, he issued another set of direct orders to all units commanding that they protect civilians and directing the removal of uncontrolled and criminal elements from HVO ranks and the use of force to prevent them from committing, what he called in his own order, "acts of terrorism." I will show you the text of this order later in my remarks. Within days, he held a press conference. At this press conference, he publicly denounced the massacre. He stated he was horrified at what had occurred at Ahmici and that he would take steps to investigate the atrocities. He further said at this press conference, "Ahmici had been done by an organised group of people under a plan controlled by someone," and he said publicly that the culprits must be found and brought to justice. He also replied to Colonel Stewart's letter, stating that he was ready to send an investigative commission into Ahmici immediately and requesting U.N. assistance to create the proper conditions for a commission to function. Continuing sniper fire from the high ground above Ahmici, as well as the general ongoing conflict, made an investigation within the Vitez enclave very difficult. No joint commission was ever formed, and although various authorities had gathered extensive information about the massacre through interviewing hundreds of survivors, that information was not shared with Tihomir Blaskic, as the authorities that had this information decided not to share any of it with the HVO concerning the massacre. Tihomir Blaskic, nonetheless, proceeded to order an HVO investigation into Ahmici. That order was given on the 10th of May, 1993. If I could have the next slide, please? That order contained the directives: "Gather all the information and submit a report on the events that actually took place in the village of Ahmici, in particular on the number of casualties, the manner in which they occurred, and the perpetrators." Paragraph 2: "I designate the assistant for SIS, Security and Information Service, of the operative zone Central Bosnia as the person responsible for this task. The deadline is 25 May, 1993." Why did he direct this order to the Security and Information Service, and I will refer back to the large chart on HVO organisation to answer my own question. Criminal investigations of military personnel are normally carried out by the military police; that is one of their principal functions. But in this instance, the military police was the unit that had been responsible for the area in which the crimes in Ahmici had occurred at the time the crimes occurred. So Tihomir Blaskic saw that it was not possible for him to direct, cause an investigation of the military police, into conduct by their own unit. Could he use the Vitez brigade? Ordinary military personnel are not competent to conduct investigative, criminal investigative activity. Particularised expertise is required. So he directed that SIS undertake an investigation and report to him within 15 days. He received that report, but Tihomir Blaskic was not satisfied with it. The report did not adequately explain how Ahmici occurred or who was responsible. So in August of 1993, he ordered a second more thorough and complete report be prepared. The second report was apparently referred to the HVO command in Mostar, HVO command or the head office for SIS. HVO Mostar subsequently sent its own investigators into Central Bosnia to conduct further investigation. These were individuals not under the command of Tihomir Blaskic. He is charged, among other things, with failure to punish the perpetrators of the Ahmici massacre. The evidence will show that he had no authority whatsoever to punish anyone in the HVO for any criminal act. His authority to sanction HVO soldiers was limited to matters pertaining to military discipline, such as desertion or a lost weapon. With respect to criminal acts, his authority was limited to the ability to refer a matter to the military police for investigation, who, in turn, would conduct an investigation and make a report to the military prosecutor. The decision to bring a charge rested solely in the hands of the military prosecutor and, of course, any decision as to guilt or innocence or sentence lay in the hands of a military court which, in fact, existed. Tihomir Blaskic had no authority to direct a military court or prosecutor to take any action. Those elements were responsible only and directly to the Department of Defence in Mostar, not to him. Mr. President, I estimate I have perhaps another hour of remarks. I wanted to tell you so that the balance of the day can be planned as you wish.
